Because of philosophical differences (an exclusively artistic program versus a broadening toward the humanities), the two couples leave the college. One note says rather that it was after the 1948 summer session for Albers and Dreier, with Charlotte Schlesinger and Trude Guermonprez also leaving.
Albers's departure creates a void that hastens the appointment of Joseph Fiore as teacher of painting and drawing, only three years after he arrived as a student.

Theodore Dreier's forced departure and the Alberses' resignation

The forced departure of Theodore Dreier, a founding member then acting treasurer, voted by a narrow majority of the faculty but in agreement with a large part of the students, sets off the resignations of Josef and Anni Albers and of several other teachers.

Amid mounting tensions threatening the central importance of the art curriculum (the institutional crisis of 1948-49), the Alberses resign; Olson, invited in fall 1948 to replace Edward Dahlberg, unknowingly becomes their successor as rector.

The Alberses and Ted Dreier leave; Fuller sees a Communist plot

Fuller interprets the changes in the college's leadership, which led him to take on a more prominent role in 1949, as an epic battle between the left and right of the Cold War. He claims that the departure of the Alberses and of Dreier (a founder and principal financial backer thanks to his wealthy family) resulted from a Communist plot to purge the old guard: Black Mountain, in his view, was probably one of the places where the cold psychological war began. In reality, the author notes, the split came from debates between training in the practical arts and courses in letters and the liberal arts.
Dahlberg writes to Albers after his departure

Four months after his departure, Dahlberg complains that Albers never answers his letters, and that when he wants such polar, solitary privacies he writes a book; he invites Albers to visit him in New York — in fact a friendly parting.
